# Summary of the 2015 UKIP Manifesto

This manifesto presents the UK Independence Party's vision for Britain as a sovereign nation freed from European Union membership, positioning the 2015 election as a historic opportunity for transformational change after a century of establishment politics.

## Core Vision and Philosophy

UKIP presents itself as fundamentally different from establishment parties, offering "fully-costed policies" rooted in national self-belief. The party argues that successive governments have failed to represent the British people's will on immigration, the economy, the NHS, and living standards. Central to their ideology is the conviction that Britain is "big enough to make our own laws" and should control its own borders while exercising fiscal responsibility.

## Economic Policy

UKIP advocates significant tax reforms including raising personal allowances to £13,000, abolishing inheritance tax, and creating a flatter income tax structure. The party proposes funding these changes through leaving the EU (saving £9 billion annually), reducing overseas aid from 0.7% to 0.2% of GNI, scrapping the HS2 rail project (saving £4 billion), and replacing the Barnett Formula. They also commit to tackling corporation tax avoidance by multinational companies and eliminating the deficit through Treasury discipline.

## Immigration

The manifesto frames immigration as an issue of "space, not race," arguing the current system is "broken" and discriminates against non-EU citizens. UKIP proposes taking back border control, implementing an Australian-style points-based system, a five-year moratorium on unskilled worker immigration, and restricting migrant access to benefits and NHS services for five years. They reject the EU's principle of free movement as incompatible with controlled immigration.

## NHS and Social Care

UKIP pledges an additional £12 billion for the NHS over five years, funding 8,000 more GPs, 20,000 nurses, and 3,000 midwives. They propose abolishing hospital parking charges, improving mental health services, and cracking down on "health tourism." The party would repeal EU directives affecting medical institutions and protect the NHS from privatisation through TTIP. Social care would receive £1.2 billion annually, with proposals for health and social care integration.

## Education

The party supports grammar schools, vocational education, and diverse school types. They would scrap Key Stage 1 SATs, reduce teacher workloads, and waive tuition fees for STEMM students who work in the UK for five years post-graduation. UKIP opposes the arbitrary 50% university attendance target and supports homeschooling and free schools.

## Brexit Roadmap

UKIP's central policy is EU withdrawal through an immediate referendum, followed by invoking Article 50 for an orderly two-year exit process. They argue Brexit would enable independent trade negotiations, restore border control, end ECJ jurisdiction, and save billions in EU contributions. The party dismisses the "three million jobs" myth as a "wilful distortion of facts."

## Other Policies

The manifesto covers housing (brownfield development, homelessness reduction), energy (repealing the Climate Change Act, supporting shale gas), defence (meeting NATO's 2% GDP commitment), political reform (citizens' initiatives, recall rights), and crime (leaving ECHR jurisdiction, creating a new Bill of Rights). UKIP promotes British cultural values while rejecting multiculturalism, and supports "trade not aid" in international development.

Throughout, UKIP positions itself as the patriotic choice for voters who believe Britain can succeed as an independent, sovereign nation rather than remaining "just a star on someone else's flag."
